name: Lighting Plots and Cue Design
title: Lighting Plots and Cue Design
answer: Lighting plots and cue design cover the placement, intensity, color, focus, and timing of lights for live performance and virtual production. In AI-assisted practice, this includes generating plot layouts from set geometry, predicting cue sequences from script or score, and simulating lighting states in real time. The field spans traditional theater, broadcast, film virtual sets, and interactive installations.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: AI lighting tools typically run on standard workstation GPUs for real-time preview and on cloud render farms for high-fidelity simulation. They integrate with lighting consoles and visualizers through protocols like DMX, Art-Net, and sACN, and with game engines such as Unreal Engine for virtual sets. Data flows from CAD or BIM models of the stage, photometric files for fixtures, and recorded cue lists.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work often begins with a designer placing fixtures in a 3D model, then using AI to propose beam angles, color palettes, or focus positions that match a reference image or mood. Cue design uses machine learning to align lighting changes with musical beats, dialogue, or blocking, and to smooth transitions between states. Designers review and adjust the AI's suggestions, keeping final creative control.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions center on who owns a generated lighting plot or cue sequence, especially when the AI is trained on prior productions or fixture libraries. Risk includes unsafe rigging suggestions if the model does not account for physical load limits, and bias toward familiar looks from training data. Provenance matters for touring shows and union contracts, where a human designer's sign-off is often required.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: AI is moving toward live adaptive lighting that responds to performer movement and audience reaction without pre-programmed cues. Virtual production will likely see tighter coupling between LED volumes, camera tracking, and AI-driven lighting to keep real and virtual elements consistent. The role of the lighting designer may shift toward curating and supervising AI systems rather than plotting every channel by hand.
